'''Great Mills''' was a British [[DIY stores|DIY retailer]], consisting of around 98 stores across the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite web |date=7 December 2000 |title=Do It All takes over Great Mills for £285m |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2000/dec/07/9 |accessdate=28 July 2022 |website=theguardian.com}}</ref> The business was bought by [[Focus DIY]] in December 2000 for £285m, who had also previously acquired [[Payless DIY]] and [[Do It All]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/1058008.stm|title=Do-it-All sees room for improvement|website=bbc.co.uk|date=6 December 2000|accessdate=20 December 2020}}</ref>

==History==
[[Image:GreatMillsStoreFront.jpg|thumb|left|A Great Mills storefront]]

Originally known as Clapton Building Supplies, the first store at [[Paulton]], Somerset in 1972 was officially opened by [[Tony Blackburn]], an unwell [[Dulux#Dulux dog|Dulux Dog]] and a staff of four.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/brizzlebornandbred/6901438191/|title=1972 Opening of Great Mills DIY store. Paulton, Somerset by radio personality Tony Blackburn|website=Flickr|accessdate=15 January 2017}}</ref> The store had a modest turnover of £50,000 but within six months, the turnover had doubled.<ref name="history">{{cite web|url=http://www.greatmills.co.uk/history.html|title=History|website=Greatmills.co.uk|accessdate=28 July 2016 |url-status=bot: unknown|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20010331035727/http://www.greatmills.co.uk/history.html|archivedate=31 March 2001}}</ref>

In the beginning of the 1990s, Great Mills launched Bay6 (Basics). These stores were identical in size, look and layout to those of rival retailer [[Wickes]]. Wickes bought the six Bay6 stores in 1995 from Great Mills' parent company, [[RMC_Group|RMC]]. Four were already trading, and two were under construction.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://academic.oup.com/rpc/article-abstract/115/20/698/1579703|title=WICKES PLC'S TRADE MARK APPLICATION|website=academic.oup.com|accessdate=18 April 2022|date=1 October 1998}}</ref>

An important step forward for the company came in 1992, with the introduction of a new central distribution method of delivering products to its stores. This saved many motorway miles as deliveries were coordinated, rather than having hundreds of suppliers delivering to the same store each day. 

Of the product range, over 70% was delivered by the Great Mills fleet in 2000 two or three times weekly. 

Some of the worst-performing Great Mills stores, at [[St. Austell]], [[Salisbury]] and [[Northallerton]], were rebranded in 1994 into the No Frills DIY chain. Other than external signage saying No Frills, the interior of the stores followed no corporate planning as the concept was to sell anything and everything in an attempt to make the loss-making store profitable again. Only St. Austell got close to being in profit before the entire chain was shut with the sale of Great Mills. Whilst none of the stores made a profit before closure, they did significantly reduce their losses.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://c7.staticflickr.com/8/7136/7526772766_20bc8b7d83_z.jpg|title=No Frills DIY|website=staticflickr.com|date=1994|accessdate=20 December 2020}}</ref>

To further reduce distribution costs, a new Central Distribution Centre was opened in July 1997. The purpose-built development was fully automated and used computer systems to monitor stock control and to make sure deliveries were made on time to stores. 

In May 1998, Great Mills appointed Jill Keen from [[Asda]] as marketing director, taking over from Peter Bastin.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/61095/diy-chain-great-mills-lures-asda-boss-key-role|title=DIY chain Great Mills lures Asda boss to key role|website=campaignlive.co.uk|accessdate=1 March 2017|date=21 May 1998}}</ref>

=== Sale to Focus DIY ===
RMC Group put Great Mills up for sale in 2000, as chief executive Peter Young said the business "is not a core part of what we do".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/news/rmc-considers-selling-great-mills-diy-chain-283032.html|title=RMC considers selling Great Mills DIY chain|website=independent.co.uk|accessdate=28 February 2017|date=16 March 2000}}</ref> Later that year, the business was acquired by [[Focus DIY|Focus Do It All]], after they switched their attentions from [[Homebase]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/4470658/Focus-abandons-Homebase-chase.html|title=Focus abandons Homebase chase|website=telegraph.co.uk|accessdate=28 February 2017|date=30 October 2000}}</ref> The Great Mill stores were all externally rebranded, though some retained parts of the interior branding.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/4474601/Great-Mills-goes-to-Focus-for-285m.html|title=Great Mills goes to Focus for £285m|website=telegraph.co.uk|accessdate=28 February 2017|date=7 December 2000}}</ref> Great Mills had almost 100 stores in the UK at the time of the proposed sale

In 2011, Focus DIY entered administration.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/news/focus-diy-falls-into-administration-as-debt-crisis-mounts-2279084.html|title=Focus DIY falls into administration as debt crisis mounts|website=independent.co.uk|accessdate=19 March 2022|date=5 May 2011}}</ref> Some of the ex-Great Mills were sold off to other retailers, while others were left empty. The original Great Mill flagship store in [[Paulton]] stood empty until 2015, when it became an outlet for [[Wickes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.insightdiy.co.uk/news/wickes-opens-in-former-focus-diy-store-in-somerset/4347.htm|title=Wickes opens in former Focus DIY store in Somerset|website=www.insightdiy.co.uk|accessdate=7 September 2020|date=7 October 2015}}</ref>
